q: Moving an estate between tiers of the 1855 reds needed something the trade could not grant on its own. What instrument finally did it in 1973?
accept: a decree from the agriculture minister
a decree of the minister of agriculture
exp: Baron Philippe pressed for fifty years and the change came by decree of the agriculture ministry, not by any vote of brokers. That is precisely why nobody expects a second one: there is no standing mechanism, only a political act.

q: Graves drew up its own classification for reds in 1953 and finished the job with whites in 1959. How is the resulting list arranged?
opts: One tier only, with estates listed for red, white or both
Two lettered categories, A and B
Three tiers reviewed every ten years
Five tiers, deliberately mirroring the 1855 reds
exp: There is no hierarchy inside it: an estate is a Cru Classe de Graves or it is not, and the entry records which colour it was classified for. Haut-Brion is classified for its red alone, so its white, one of the most expensive dry whites in France, carries no rank at all.

q: Two bottles from the same Right Bank village read Saint-Emilion Grand Cru and Saint-Emilion Grand Cru Classe. What separates them?
opts: The first is an appellation, the second is a rank held by a named estate
The first is a rank, the second is a wine from purchased fruit
The first is declassified wine from a classified estate, the second is the grand vin
They are two spellings of one thing and mean the same
exp: Saint-Emilion Grand Cru is open to anyone in the zone who meets lower yields, higher minimum alcohol and a longer elevage with an approval tasting. Grand Cru Classe is a place on the classification, held by a specific chateau, and the word Classe is the entire difference on the shelf.

q: Every estate on the Graves classified list now sits inside a single appellation carved out in 1987. Which appellation contains them all?
exp: The classified estates all lie in the northern communes nearest the city, which is exactly the ground the 1987 appellation was drawn around. Nothing in the southern half of Graves was ever classified, so the two lists coincide entirely.

q: Rebuilt after its own annulment, the Medoc ranking outside 1855 now runs to three ascending levels. Name them in order.
accept: cru bourgeois cru bourgeois superieur and cru bourgeois exceptionnel
cru bourgeois cru bourgeois superieur cru bourgeois exceptionnel
cru bourgeois cru bourgeois superieur and exceptionnel
cru bourgeois then superieur then exceptionnel
ans: Cru Bourgeois, Cru Bourgeois Superieur and Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel
exp: The tiers were abolished in the 2000s after litigation, leaving a flat annual selection of individual wines, and were restored when the system was rebuilt around estate-level assessment. Exceptionnel is the smallest group and carries requirements on vineyard management and cellar practice, not only on the tasting.

q: Unlike an 1855 growth, a Cru Bourgeois estate holds its standing only for a fixed run of harvests before it must reapply. How long does the award now run?
exp: Reapplication is the whole point of the exercise: the rank is meant to describe present performance rather than a nineteenth-century price list. It also means the label statement is tied to the vintage in the bottle, not to the chateau in perpetuity.

q: Ausone and Cheval Blanc held the top rank of the Saint-Emilion classification alone for decades. In the 2012 revision, which two estates were raised to join them?
exp: Both promotions were contested in court, which is the recurring feature of this classification rather than an accident: because rank is revisable it is worth suing over, and because it is written into the appellation rules the state ends up in the argument. The 1855 list attracts no litigation for the opposite reason.

q: Only one of the Medoc's great communal appellations extends well beyond the village that names it. Which group of communes does Margaux also cover?
exp: Five communes in all share the name, which is much of why Margaux is the least uniform of the four in soil and in style. An address in Cantenac or Labarde is labelled Margaux with nothing on the bottle to say so.

q: One of the four famous Medoc communes holds no First Growth at all, yet nearly all of its vineyard is classified. Which commune is that?
exp: Saint-Julien is small, tightly drawn and dominated by classified estates, so the average bottle carrying the name is a serious wine. Saint-Estephe is larger and has proportionally far more unclassified land, which is why its name alone tells you less.

q: Wines from the northernmost of the four great communes are firmer and slower than their neighbours because a water-retaining layer sits under the gravel. Name that layer.
exp: Saint-Estephe's gravel is shallower and the clay under it holds water, so the vine suffers less drought stress and the wines carry more flesh and more grip. Latour's Enclos in Pauillac shows the same effect in miniature, which is one reason it performs in dry years.

q: Great Medoc sites are almost all built on a low mound of gravel standing a few metres proud of the surrounding land. What is the local term for such a mound?
exp: The height is trivial in absolute terms and decisive in practice: it puts the water table further below the roots and lets cold air drain away downslope. The old Medoc saying that the best vines see the river is really a statement about being on a croupe.

q: Running north from the city, the Haut-Medoc appellation stops where the plain Medoc appellation begins. Which commune marks that northern boundary?
accept: the commune of saint seurin de cadourne
exp: North of it the peninsula flattens, the gravel thins and clay takes over, which is the physical reason the line falls where it does. Everything beyond is entitled only to Medoc, whatever the quality in the glass.

q: A Pauillac estate bottles a white wine from Sauvignon Blanc grown among its Cabernet. Which appellation must that bottle carry?
exp: Every communal appellation in the Medoc is for red wine only, so a white from Pauillac drops straight to the regional level however grand the address. Mouton's Aile d'Argent and the white of Margaux are sold exactly this way.

q: Four existing cotes appellations were folded into a single umbrella denomination in 2009, each keeping its own name as a prefix. Which four?
opts: Castillon, Francs, Bourg and Graves de Vayres
exp: Sainte-Foy joined the union later and Cotes de Bourg stayed out of it altogether, which is the detail that catches people. A wine may also be sold as plain Cotes de Bordeaux without any prefix if the fruit is blended across the zones.

q: Two communal appellations of the Medoc sit inland behind the main gravel ridge and hold no classified growth between them. Which pair?
exp: Both are entitled to their own communal names, so they outrank the surrounding Haut-Medoc while sitting outside the 1855 story entirely. Their clay and limestone gives sterner, less immediately charming wine, which is much of why the brokers of 1855 priced them below the riverside communes.

q: A modest stream runs east to west across the Right Bank, marking the northern limit of Pomerol and of Saint-Emilion, with the satellite appellations lying beyond it. Name that stream.
exp: It is small enough to step across and it is nonetheless one of the most consequential lines in Bordeaux, because Lalande-de-Pomerol and the four Saint-Emilion satellites all begin on the far side of it. Old local lore held that the good wine was on the southern bank and the witches on the northern one.
